title: GOD DIDN’T WAIT FOR YOU TO BECOME STRONG—HE WAS WAITING FOR YOU TO STOP PRETENDING YOU WERE
paragraphs: GOD DIDN’T WAIT FOR YOU TO BECOME STRONG—HE WAS WAITING FOR YOU TO STOP PRETENDING YOU WERE

What if the weakness you keep begging God to remove is the very place where Jesus wants to reveal His power? The heartbreaking, hope-restoring truth behind 2 Corinthians 12:9 that could change how you see your suffering, your failures, and the grace that has been carrying you all along.
There is a kind of exhaustion that sleep cannot fix.
You can spend eight hours in bed and still wake up tired.
You can smile in photographs, answer messages, attend church, worship with your hands raised, and tell everyone that God is good.
And you believe He is.
But somewhere beneath that smile, there is a question you are almost ashamed to ask.
Lord, if You are really with me, why am I still struggling like this?
Why am I still fighting the same temptation?
Why does the anxiety return?
Why does the grief still hurt?
Why does my faith sometimes feel so small?
Why have I prayed so many times about something that still has not changed?
And perhaps the most painful question of all...
What is wrong with me that I cannot seem to become the Christian I thought I would be by now?
You have heard sermons about victory.
You have read testimonies about breakthroughs.
You have watched other believers celebrate answered prayers while you quietly wondered whether heaven had somehow overlooked yours.
You love Jesus.
You really do.
But you are tired of being strong.
And there is something I desperately want you to understand before you read another word.
Your weakness has not caught Jesus by surprise.
He knew about the tears you would hide.
He knew about the battles you would struggle to explain.
He knew about the prayers you would whisper through clenched teeth when you had nothing eloquent left to say.
And He did not wait until you became impressive before deciding to love you.
In fact, one of the most extraordinary declarations in the entire New Testament was given to a man who had begged God to take his suffering away.
And God said no.
Not because He was cruel.
Not because He was indifferent.

But because there was something the apostle Paul needed to discover about the power of Christ that he might never have understood in the same way if his prayer had been answered exactly as he requested.
Listen carefully.
This is not a story about how weakness becomes strength through positive thinking.
This is not permission to romanticize suffering.
And it is certainly not a promise that every painful circumstance will disappear if you believe hard enough.
This is something far more breathtaking.
It is the story of a Savior whose power is sufficient even when His servant remains weak.
And once you understand it, you may never look at your own broken places the same way again.
Paul was not a stranger to the supernatural.
He had encountered the risen Christ.
He had preached the Gospel across cities and cultures.
He had witnessed God's extraordinary work.
He had endured persecution, imprisonment, beatings, shipwrecks, hunger, and danger for the sake of Jesus.
If anyone could have been tempted to believe that spiritual maturity meant becoming untouchable, Paul had the credentials.
Yet in 2 Corinthians 12, he reveals something deeply personal.
He had been given what he called a thorn in the flesh.
The Greek expression is σκόλοψ τῇ σαρκί (skolops tē sarki).
The word skolops can refer to a sharp stake or thorn, an image of something painfully piercing and persistent.
Paul never identifies the thorn with enough precision for us to know exactly what it was.
Some have suggested a physical illness. Others have proposed persecution or another severe affliction.
But Scripture does not settle the question.
And we must not pretend to know what God has not revealed.
What we do know is that Paul suffered.
Not mildly.
Not conveniently.
Not in a way he could simply ignore.
He describes the thorn as something that tormented him, and he says it was permitted to keep him from becoming conceited because of the extraordinary revelations he had received.
Paul even calls it a messenger of Satan sent to harass him.
That detail matters.
The passage does not teach that suffering is automatically good or that evil becomes holy because God can work through it.
It shows that God's sovereign purpose can prevail even amid what is painful and hostile.
Then Paul makes a confession that should comfort every believer who has ever prayed the same prayer repeatedly.
He asked the Lord three times to remove it.
Three times.
The great apostle prayed for relief.
The man who taught churches about faith and perseverance asked God to take away his affliction.
He did not pretend the pain was pleasant.
He did not call his suffering imaginary.
He did not consider asking for deliverance a failure of faith.
Paul wanted the thorn gone.
And there is no shame in that.
If you are praying for healing, you are not necessarily demonstrating weak faith.

If you are asking God to restore your marriage, free you from an addiction, help you endure depression, or open a door that has remained painfully closed, you are not wrong to bring those desires before Him.
Jesus Himself, in Gethsemane, prayed that the cup of suffering might pass from Him, while submitting Himself perfectly to the Father's will (Matthew 26:39).
Faith is not pretending that pain does not hurt.
Faith brings pain into the presence of God.
But here is where Paul's story becomes unforgettable.
God did not give Paul the answer he wanted.
He gave him a promise greater than Paul had understood.
In 2 Corinthians 12:9, the Lord declares:
“My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness.”
That is the wording of the King James Version.
Now listen to the original Greek:
Ἀρκεῖ σοι ἡ χάρις μου, ἡ γὰρ δύναμις ἐν ἀσθενείᾳ τελεῖται.
Arkei soi hē charis mou, hē gar dynamis en astheneia teleitai.
A close translation is:
“My grace is sufficient for you, for power is brought to completion in weakness.”
Do not rush past those words.
The Greek verb ἀρκεῖ (arkei) means “is sufficient” or “is enough.”
God was not telling Paul that his pain was insignificant.
He was telling him that divine grace would not prove inadequate.
The word χάρις (charis) means grace—God's freely given favor and help.
Not something Paul could earn.
Not something he could manufacture through religious performance.
Not a reward for finally becoming strong enough.
Grace.
And then comes the phrase that changes everything.
ἡ δύναμις ἐν ἀσθενείᾳ τελεῖται
Hē dynamis en astheneia teleitai.
“Power is brought to completion in weakness.”
The word δύναμις (dynamis) refers to power or ability.
ἀσθένεια (astheneia) refers to weakness, frailty, or lack of strength.
And τελεῖται (teleitai), from teleō, carries the idea of being completed, accomplished, or brought to its intended goal.
The point is not that God's power was previously defective and needed human weakness to improve it.
God has never lacked power.
The point is that Christ's power reaches its intended expression in Paul's situation precisely where Paul's own sufficiency fails.
The weakness does not create God's power.
It becomes the setting in which His power is displayed.
And suddenly the entire conversation changes.
Paul had been asking, Lord, when will You remove what makes me weak?
Christ answered, in effect, My grace is enough for you even here.
That is not the answer our flesh naturally wants.
We want God to make us so strong that we never tremble.
Sometimes He teaches us to trust Him while we are trembling.
We want Him to remove every reason we might fall.
He teaches us to depend upon the One who is able to keep us.
We want a testimony that says, “Look how powerful I became.”
But the Gospel produces a testimony that says, “Look how faithful Jesus has been.”
And perhaps this is where the words become painfully personal.
Because there are people reading this who have spent years trying to appear spiritually stronger than they feel.
You know the language.
“I'm blessed.”
“God is good.”
“Everything happens for a reason.”
And sometimes those words express genuine faith.
But sometimes they become a hiding place.
A way to avoid admitting that you are hurting.
A way to make sure nobody sees the fear behind your confidence.
You have learned how to encourage others while quietly falling apart.
You have become the person everyone calls for prayer, yet you struggle to ask anyone to pray for you.
You tell others to trust God while lying awake at night wondering how you will survive another month.
And when the tears finally come, you feel guilty.
As though a mature Christian should have outgrown the need to cry.
But consider the apostle Paul.
He did not become less faithful by acknowledging his weakness.
He became more explicit about his dependence on Christ.
After hearing the Lord's answer, Paul wrote:
“Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me.” (2 Corinthians 12:9, KJV)
That word rest is remarkable.
The Greek verb ἐπισκηνώσῃ (episkēnōsē) conveys the image of dwelling over or taking up residence upon someone.
Paul's language suggests the power of Christ resting upon him, like a sheltering presence.
Not because Paul had become invincible.
But because Christ remained sufficient.
Imagine the difference.
You have spent your life thinking that weakness means God has moved away.
Paul discovered that weakness could become the very place where Christ's sustaining power was especially evident.
You have been measuring God's nearness by how quickly the storm ends.
But the Lord's promise to Paul was not that every storm would immediately end.
It was that His grace would be sufficient in the storm.
The absence of immediate deliverance is not proof of the absence of divine love.
Read that again.
Because someone needs to stop interpreting an unanswered prayer as a rejection.
God's answer to Paul was not the removal of the thorn.
It was the assurance of sufficient grace.
That does not mean God never heals.
Scripture testifies that He does.
It does not mean you should stop praying for change.
Paul prayed. Jesus taught His disciples to pray persistently.
And it does not mean you should remain in abuse, neglect your health, refuse treatment, or ignore practical help.
Biblical dependence on God is not the rejection of wise action.
Sometimes grace reaches us through a physician, a counselor, a trusted pastor, a supportive friend, or a necessary decision to seek safety.
The promise of Christ's sufficiency does not require us to deny the ordinary means through which God provides care.
But it does confront the belief that our worth, spiritual standing, or usefulness to God depends on never appearing weak.
And that belief has wounded more Christians than many of us realize.
Somewhere along the way, we began confusing spiritual maturity with emotional invulnerability.
We started treating every struggle as evidence that something was wrong with our relationship with God.
We made room for testimonies of victory but very little room for the long, quiet obedience of believers who were still waiting.
We celebrated the person who was healed.
But sometimes we did not know what to say to the person who continued to suffer.
We applauded the restored marriage.
But struggled to sit beside the believer whose spouse never came home.
We rejoiced over the financial miracle.
But overlooked the single parent who was still counting coins at the grocery store.
We praised God for deliverance.
And rightly so.
But we sometimes forgot that the God who delivers is also the God who sustains.
That His faithfulness is not measured solely by whether circumstances change.
That the believer who continues trusting Christ through unanswered questions is not necessarily living a lesser Christian life.
And perhaps the most powerful example of all is not Paul.
It is Jesus.
Because if we want to understand divine power revealed through what looks like weakness, we must eventually stand at the foot of the cross.
There was a moment when the Son of God hung before a mocking crowd.
His body wounded.
His hands pierced.
His enemies convinced they had won.
To human eyes, it looked like defeat.
The Messiah had been arrested.
Condemned.
Humiliated.
Crucified.
What kind of King wears a crown of thorns?
What kind of Savior allows Himself to be nailed to a cross?
What kind of victory looks like this?
But the apostle Paul later wrote:
“For though he was crucified through weakness, yet he liveth by the power of God.” (2 Corinthians 13:4, KJV)
This does not mean Jesus was morally weak or powerless.
He willingly submitted to suffering in obedience to the Father.
His crucifixion displayed apparent helplessness to the watching world, yet through His death and resurrection God accomplished redemption.
The cross was not God's plan collapsing.
It was God's saving purpose unfolding.
Jesus bore our sins.
He suffered in the place of sinners.
He died and rose again.
And through Him, forgiveness and reconciliation with God are offered to all who repent and believe.
That is why the Gospel is not a message about human beings discovering how extraordinary they already are.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ has done what sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
We could not rescue ourselves from sin.
We could not earn righteousness through religious performance.
We could not overcome death by trying harder.
We needed a Savior.
And God gave us His Son.
This is why Paul's weakness matters so profoundly.
It points beyond Paul.
It points toward the sufficiency of Christ.
The Christian life begins with grace, continues by grace, and rests upon the faithfulness of Jesus.
Our weakness is not the foundation of our salvation.
Christ is.
Our suffering does not atone for sin.
His sacrifice does.
Our perseverance does not make us our own redeemer.
Jesus alone saves.
And yet the Savior who redeemed us also promises to sustain those who belong to Him.
That is where the heart of this passage becomes almost overwhelming.
The One who died for you is not asking you to become your own savior.
He is calling you to trust Him.
Even when you cannot understand everything He allows.
Even when the answer is not yet what you hoped.
Even when obedience is difficult.
Even when you have to admit that you cannot carry the burden alone.
There is a world of difference between surrender and giving up.
Giving up says, “Nothing matters anymore.”
Surrender says, “Jesus, I cannot control everything, but I entrust myself to You.”
Giving up abandons hope.
Surrender places hope in the One who conquered the grave.
And maybe your next step of faith is not another dramatic promise that you will never struggle again.
Maybe it is a painfully sincere prayer.
Lord Jesus, I am weak. I need Your help. Forgive my sin. Teach me to trust You. Give me the grace to obey You today.
Not tomorrow.
Not for the next twenty years all at once.
Today.
Because sometimes we become so overwhelmed by the thought of surviving the entire journey that we forget God calls us to walk faithfully through the day in front of us.
The grace promised to Paul was sufficient for the weakness he faced.
And the Christ who spoke those words has not changed.
But there is another truth we must not overlook.
Weakness is not the same thing as cherished sin.
Some people hear “God's power is made perfect in weakness” and assume it means they can remain comfortable in disobedience.
That is not Paul's message.
Paul was not celebrating rebellion against God.
He was describing affliction, limitations, hardships, and dependence upon Christ.
When we fall into sin, the Gospel calls us to repentance.
When we are tempted, we are called to resist.
When we have harmed someone, grace does not excuse us from confession, restitution where appropriate, and the pursuit of reconciliation.
The power of Christ does not make holiness unnecessary.
It makes faithful obedience possible through His grace.
And when we stumble, we do not have to hide behind religious appearances.
We can come into the light.
First John 1:9 declares:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
Notice what Scripture does not say.
It does not say that God forgives only those who have become impressive.
It does not say that the door of mercy opens only after you have successfully repaired yourself.
Forgiveness rests on the faithfulness and justice of God, grounded in the saving work of Jesus Christ.
That does not make repentance optional.
It makes repentance hopeful.
You can stop pretending.
You can confess what you have been hiding.
You can turn away from what has been destroying you.
You can seek help.
You can begin walking in obedience.
Not because sin is harmless.
But because Jesus is a real Savior.
And perhaps there is someone reading this who has been carrying a particular kind of shame.
You remember what you did.
The words you said.
The trust you betrayed.
The season when you walked away from God.
The secret compromise.
The choices you wish you could undo.
You have wondered whether your past has permanently disqualified you from being loved by Christ.
And you have tried to compensate by becoming stronger, busier, more religious, more useful.
As though enough good deeds could finally silence the accusation in your heart.
But the Gospel does not say that your past was harmless.
It says that the blood of Jesus Christ is sufficient to cleanse repentant sinners.
The cross does not minimize sin.
It reveals how serious sin is—and how extraordinary God's mercy is.
The resurrection does not erase every earthly consequence of our choices.
But it announces that sin and death do not have the final word over those who belong to Christ.
This is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior.
Not because scandal is beautiful.
Not because failure should be celebrated.
Not because grace permits us to continue in darkness.
But because Jesus Christ can redeem sinners, restore the repentant, and transform lives that human judgment has already written off.
Think about Peter.
He promised loyalty to Jesus.
Then, under pressure, he denied knowing Him three times.
Imagine the sound of the rooster.
Imagine the sudden memory of Jesus' words.
Imagine the crushing realization that the courage Peter thought he possessed had failed him when it mattered most.
Luke 22:62 tells us that Peter went out and wept bitterly.
That was not a heroic moment.
It was a devastating one.
But Peter's failure was not the end of his story.
After the resurrection, Jesus restored him and entrusted him with the responsibility of caring for His sheep (John 21:15–19).
Peter did not restore himself through confidence.
He was restored by the risen Christ.
And that is the kind of grace that should bring us to our knees.
The grace that confronts our sin without abandoning the repentant sinner.
The grace that tells the truth about our failures without declaring them stronger than the Savior.
The grace that does not merely help us feel better about yesterday, but calls us into faithful obedience today.
Some of you are living in a chapter you never wanted.
You thought you would be further along by now.
You thought the marriage would be healed.
You thought your children would have returned to the faith.
You thought the medical results would be different.
You thought the grief would have become easier to carry.
You thought that after all these years of following Jesus, you would feel less afraid.
And perhaps you have begun believing that the unfinished parts of your life make your testimony less valuable.
But what if you have misunderstood what a testimony is?
A testimony is not always the story of a problem that disappeared.
Sometimes it is the story of a Savior who remained faithful while the problem persisted.
Sometimes the testimony is that you did not abandon Christ.
Sometimes it is that you repented after falling.
Sometimes it is that you asked for help instead of suffering alone.
Sometimes it is that you opened your Bible with trembling hands and whispered, Lord, I still believe. Help my unbelief.
And sometimes the testimony is not that you felt strong.
It is that Jesus sustained you when you knew you were not.
This is not an invitation to make peace with every destructive circumstance.
It is an invitation to stop making your circumstances the final authority on God's character.
The cross and resurrection reveal His saving love more clearly than the temporary condition of your life ever could.
And this brings us to Paul's extraordinary conclusion.
He writes in 2 Corinthians 12:10:
That sounds like a contradiction until we understand the source of the strength.
Paul was not saying that weakness magically turns into human ability.
He was saying that when he recognized his own limitations, he could rely more fully on the power of Christ.
His confidence had shifted.
Away from self-sufficiency.
Toward the Savior.
Away from personal greatness.
Toward divine grace.
Away from the illusion that he could control every outcome.
Toward the faithfulness of the Lord who had called him.
And maybe that is the shift some of us desperately need.
Not a smaller view of suffering.
But a greater view of Jesus.
Not denial of our limitations.
But deeper dependence upon His grace.
Not pride in how much we can endure.
But gratitude for the One who carries us through what we could never face alone.
And if these words have reached a place in your heart that you rarely allow anyone to see, I want to invite you to respond with something more meaningful than a casual reaction.
You do not have to tell the whole world every detail of your pain.
You do not owe strangers your private struggles.
But perhaps your honest response will remind another weary believer that they are not the only one still learning how to depend upon Christ.
Someone may be praying tonight for the very endurance God has already taught you.
There is another reason I am asking you to do something with this message.
Because somewhere on your Facebook friends list is a person who looks perfectly fine.
They post photographs.
They laugh.
They go to work.
They care for their families.
They attend church.
But you do not know what happens when the room becomes quiet.
You do not know what they have been praying about.
You do not know how close they may be to giving up.
Not to prove that you are religious.
Not to impress anyone.
But because the Gospel deserves to be heard beyond the walls of our churches and the boundaries of our comfort.
A simple share can place Scripture before someone who might never have searched for it.
We also want to invite you into something deeper than reading one powerful message and moving on.
These resources are intended to help you study the Word, strengthen your understanding of the Gospel, and develop a more faithful walk with the Lord.
Because emotional encouragement matters.
But lasting discipleship requires more than a moment of inspiration.
We need Scripture.
We need sound teaching.
We need prayer.
We need Christian community.
We need the continual work of the Holy Spirit conforming us to the image of Christ.
And this is where I want to make a personal invitation.
It is one practical way to participate in making these resources available to others.
Christians can glorify God through prayer, obedience, generosity, service, sharing the Gospel, caring for the vulnerable, and faithfully supporting their local churches.
Giving should be voluntary, thoughtful, and sincere.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 teaches:
“God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
It should come from a willing heart and the conviction that this ministry's work is worth helping sustain.
Think about that.
A believer with limited resources may still be able to read a devotional.
A struggling Christian may discover a free book that helps them understand the Bible.
A seeker may encounter a Gospel-centered article at exactly the moment they are willing to listen.
We cannot promise what every reader will do with those opportunities.
But we can faithfully make the truth available.
They are not substitutes for Scripture, church fellowship, or genuine discipleship.
You are still welcome here.
You can still read.
You can still pray.
You can still share.
And you can still make use of the free discipleship resources available through the ministry.
The grace of God is not merchandise.
And the Gospel must never be placed behind a price tag.
That is precisely why voluntary support matters.
It helps sustain work that seeks to make biblical encouragement and discipleship resources accessible to more people.
But now, before you leave this article, I want to return to the person who first began reading it.
The person who was tired.
The person who wondered whether God was disappointed.
The person who has been secretly comparing their private struggles with everyone else's public victories.
The person who has prayed for the thorn to disappear.
Maybe your circumstances will change tomorrow.
Maybe God will bring the breakthrough you have been asking for.
Maybe healing will come through a long process.
Maybe reconciliation will require years of patience and repentance.
Maybe some questions will remain unanswered in this life.
I cannot promise you which outcome God has appointed.
Scripture does not give me permission to make promises He has not made.
But I can point you to the promise Christ gave Paul.
“My grace is sufficient for thee.”
Not because Paul was strong enough.
Not because his suffering was easy.
Not because the thorn no longer mattered.
But because Jesus was enough to sustain him in the weakness he could not remove.
And that same risen Christ is worthy of your trust.
You do not have to earn His attention through perfection.
You do not have to hide your tears to prove your faith.
You do not have to pretend that every wound has healed.
You are called to come to Him in repentance and faith, to receive His grace, and to follow Him in the strength He provides.
And if you have never truly surrendered your life to Jesus Christ, do not mistake familiarity with Christian language for saving faith.
The invitation of the Gospel is personal.
Turn from sin.
Believe in the crucified and risen Savior.
Entrust yourself to Him.
Follow Him.
Not because He promises a life without pain.
But because He alone gives forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and eternal life.
And if you already belong to Christ but have grown weary, perhaps your prayer tonight can be very simple.
Jesus, I am tired.
I have tried to carry things You never asked me to carry alone.
I have hidden my weakness because I was afraid of being judged.
I have sometimes trusted my ability more than Your grace.
Forgive me.
Teach me to depend on You.
Give me wisdom to seek the help I need, courage to obey Your Word, and strength to remain faithful.
If You choose to remove this thorn, I will thank You.
And if You call me to endure it longer, sustain me by Your grace.
Let my life point people not to my greatness, but to Yours.
In Jesus' name, amen.
And now I want to leave you with one final thought.
When Paul asked God to remove the thorn, he was asking for a different circumstance.
When Christ answered him, He revealed a deeper sufficiency.
The thorn did not become Paul's identity.
His weakness did not become his savior.
Jesus remained Lord.
Jesus remained sufficient.
Jesus remained the source of his strength.
And that is the hope I want you to carry away from these words.
Your story may contain chapters you would never have chosen.
There may be consequences you cannot reverse, losses you cannot explain, wounds that require time and care, and weaknesses you wish nobody knew about.
But if you belong to Jesus Christ, those things do not have the authority to redefine the Gospel.
His cross is still sufficient.
His resurrection is still victorious.
His mercy is still real.
His Word is still true.
And His grace is not exhausted by the fact that you need it again today.
So when the night becomes quiet and your strength feels small, remember what the Lord told Paul.
Not, “You are strong enough without Me.”
But, “My grace is sufficient for you.”
The thorn may still be there tomorrow—but it will never be greater than the Savior who holds you today.
